abstract: Pup ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) are thought to communicate and elicit maternal care, yet the structure of the pup call repertoire and how it changes across the vulnerable first postnatal week remain poorly characterized. Here we analyzed approximately 59,000 USVs emitted by wildtype mouse pups (postnatal days P0-P5) during a pup retrieval paradigm that included habituation, pup isolation, and retrieval phases, performed with wild-type (WT) and Mecp2-heterozygous (Het) female mice as alloparental surrogates. Using DeepSqueak-based acoustic feature extraction and unsupervised clustering, we identified eight distinct call types, grouped into two broad classes based on shared acoustic properties. The relative prevalence and sequencing of these call types shifted systematically with postnatal age and behavioral phase, indicating that the pup vocal repertoire is both developmentally and contextually dynamic during the first postnatal week. However, call-type composition and acoustic characteristics did not differ with behavioral outcome, consistent with the model in which USVs function as general arousal signals integrated with other sensory cues. A candidate sequence-level pattern distinguished failed retrievals but was based on few calls and requires further validation. Pup call repertoire and developmental trajectory were also indistinguishable between WT and Het surrogates, indicating that the previously reported retrieval deficit in Het females does not arise from atypical pup vocal signals. Together, these results provide a detailed developmental and contextual map of the early pup call repertoire and a framework for relating call-type dynamics to auditory circuit plasticity across early postnatal life.
